ai_summary:
Great Britain's wind fleet is generating 16.8 GW, with estimated Scottish wind output providing 5.7 GW, accounting for 56.4% of installed Scottish wind capacity. Thanks to this robust renewable production, Scottish carbon intensity sits at 0 gCO2/kWh compared to 70 gCO2/kWh GB-wide. However, severe cross-border transmission constraints prevent this zero-carbon energy from reaching demand centers further south. Consequently, Scottish generation curtailed so far today has reached 24.9 GWh, incurring an immediate constraint cost of £1,370,516. To compensate for this stranded green energy, thermal generation stepped in down south, consuming an estimated 4,728,454 cubic meters of gas and releasing an additional 8,710 tonnes of CO2. 

If today’s curtailment pace reflects typical ongoing friction, the annualized impact points to an estimated yearly cost of £500 million. Apportioning this sum across Great Britain’s typical annual power consumption of approximately 300 million MWh, Scottish network bottlenecks add an estimated burden of £1.70/MWh to every consumer invoice in the UK. This analysis demonstrates the dual financial and environmental penalty of curtailing zero-carbon Scottish wind while burning costly fossil fuels elsewhere.
